text: Your blind spot is real. Where the optic nerve leaves each eye there are no light receptors at all, and your brain quietly fills the gap with whatever surrounds it.
The magical number seven is out of date. George Miller's 1956 paper suggested people hold about seven items in mind at once; later work by Nelson Cowan puts the real limit nearer four chunks.
Wilhelm Wundt opened what is usually called the first psychology laboratory, in Leipzig, in 1879.
In the 1999 'invisible gorilla' study, about half of the viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.
The claim that we use only 10% of our brains is a myth. Brain scans show activity across virtually the whole brain, even during sleep.
Learning styles have little support. Studies that match teaching to a student's preferred 'visual' or 'auditory' style generally find no improvement in learning.
Kitty Genovese's murder in 1964 was reported as having 38 silent witnesses. Later reporting found far fewer people saw the attack, and at least one called the police.

Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables like 'DAX' and 'BOK' and charted how fast he forgot them. His forgetting curve, published in 1885, was the first careful measurement of memory.
'We are what we repeatedly do' is often credited to Aristotle, but it comes from Will Durant's 1926 summary of Aristotle's ideas.
More choice can make choosing harder. In a 2000 study, shoppers offered 24 jams were less likely to buy one than shoppers offered 6, though later studies found the effect is often small.
Most people who lose a limb still feel it afterwards, sometimes for years, because the brain's map of the body keeps the missing part.
Nobody yet knows exactly why we dream. Theories range from sorting memories to rehearsing threats, and none has won.
Try naming the ink colour, not the word: reading 'RED' printed in blue slows you down. This is the Stroop effect, described by John Ridley Stroop in 1935.
Deja vu is common. In surveys, roughly two-thirds of people say they've experienced it.
During the Second World War, B. F. Skinner trained pigeons to steer missiles in a scheme called Project Pigeon. It was never used in combat.

The Muller-Lyer illusion, two equal lines that look different lengths because of the arrowheads at their ends, fools people from some cultures less than others, which suggests experience shapes even basic perception.
The Dunning-Kruger effect is often misdescribed. The 1999 study found that low scorers overestimated themselves, but some later work argues part of the pattern is a statistical artefact.
Newborns recognise their mother's voice within days of birth, and in experiments they prefer it to the voices of other women.
Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his head in 1848. His reported change in personality became a founding case for the idea that parts of the brain have specific jobs.
In a 1998 experiment, about half of people giving directions to a stranger didn't notice when the stranger was swapped for a different person mid-conversation.
The cocktail party effect is why you can tune out a noisy room yet still catch your own name across it. Colin Cherry studied it in 1953.
Placebos can help even when people know they're taking one. Open-label placebo trials have reported benefits for conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome.
Why we yawn is still debated. Contagious yawning is real, but whether yawns cool the brain or tell others we're tired is unresolved.
Hermann Rorschach published his inkblot test in 1921 and died the following year, aged 37.

Memory rebuilds rather than replays. In Elizabeth Loftus's 1974 study, people told that cars 'smashed' into each other estimated higher speeds than people told they 'hit', and more of them later remembered broken glass that wasn't there.
'The mind is not a vessel to be filled, but a fire to be kindled' is usually credited to Plutarch, but it's a loose paraphrase of what he actually wrote.
Your gut has hundreds of millions of neurons of its own, which is why it's sometimes called the second brain.
Trying not to think of a white bear makes you think of it more. Daniel Wegner showed this rebound effect in a 1987 experiment.
Seeing faces in clouds and plug sockets has a name: pareidolia. Brain scans show face-sensitive areas responding to these false faces in a fraction of a second.
Sleep helps you keep what you learned. People who sleep after learning remember more than people kept awake, because sleep helps consolidate new memories.

Mary Whiton Calkins finished all the requirements for a Harvard PhD in 1895, but Harvard refused to award it because she was a woman. She later became the first woman president of the American Psychological Association.
